usage: 근무하다 takes the workplace with 에서 (the place where activity happens), never 에: 회사에서 근무해요.
Frozen noun chunk — 근무 stands alone as a noun here; memorize 주 5일 근무 / 주말 근무 as fixed phrases.
재택(在宅) 'at-home' + 근무; written as one word. Boomed post-2020, so you'll hear it constantly now.
야간(夜間) 'night' + 근무; this is the scheduled-shift sense, contrasted with 야근 (staying late once).
examples: 저는 은행에서 근무해요.
I work at a bank.
Simplest self-introduction frame: 〈place〉에서 근무해요 — polished and resume-friendly.
몇 시부터 몇 시까지 근무하세요?
From what time to what time do you work?
부터…까지 frames a span; 근무하다 sounds more professional than 일하다 when asking a colleague's hours.
다음 달부터 다른 지점에서 근무하게 됐어요.
Starting next month I'll be working at a different branch.
-게 됐어요 signals the transfer was decided by circumstance, not your own choice — humble and natural.
nuance: 근무하다 is the workplace word for 'to work / be on duty', focused on your employment and shift rather than the physical act of doing tasks. The hanja is 勤務 (勤 'diligence/service' + 務 'duty'), so it literally means 'serve one's duty' — that institutional flavor is why it dominates contracts, ID badges, and self-introductions. The sharp contrast is with 일하다: 일하다 is the everyday, hands-on 'do work' you say to friends, while 근무하다 is about being formally posted somewhere, so a soldier, a 9-to-5 office worker, or a clerk 근무한다 at a location. Habitual collocations are all fixed nouns: 주 5일 근무, 재택근무, 야간 근무, 근무 시간 (working hours), 근무 환경 (work environment). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: the workplace takes 에서 (location of an activity), so it is 회사에서 근무해요, never 회사에 근무해요 or 회사를 근무해요. Also do not reach for 근무하다 to describe doing a single chore — that is 하다 or 일하다.

Don't use 근무하다 for a one-off task like tidying your desk — 근무하다 is about being employed / on shift, not doing a specific chore; use 일하다 or just 하다 there.

usage: to be in charge of a project
The thing you are responsible for takes the object particle 을/를: 프로젝트를 담당해요.
Derived noun 담당 + 자(者) 'person'; ubiquitous in offices and customer service: 담당자분께 전달할게요.
담당 used attributively before a noun = 'the ~ one is responsible for'; 담당 부서 = the department in charge.
Pairs with department names (영업/마케팅/회계 등); states which function is officially yours.
examples: 제가 이 일을 담당해요.
I'm in charge of this task.
Bare, clear role statement; 을/를 on the task, 제가 to spotlight that it's you.
이 건은 누가 담당하세요?
Who is in charge of this matter?
이 건 = 'this case/matter', standard office wording for routing a question to the right person.
저는 해외 거래처를 담당하고 있습니다.
I'm in charge of our overseas clients.
-고 있습니다 = formal ongoing duty; right register for an email or a meeting.
nuance: 담당하다 means to officially be responsible for a specific task, client, or functional area at work. The hanja 擔當 is 擔 'to shoulder/carry' + 當 'to take on', so it literally pictures shouldering an assigned load — which is why it feels institutional and ongoing rather than a one-time effort. Compare it with its near-synonym 맡다: 맡다 is the warm, personal, often volunteered 'I'll take this on', whereas 담당하다 is the cool, official 'this is formally assigned to me', the version you put on a name card or org chart. The single most useful spin-off is the noun 담당자 ('the person in charge'), heard everywhere in offices and call centers (담당자분께 전달하겠습니다). Natural collocations: 업무를 담당하다, 마케팅을 담당하다, 담당 부서, 담당 구역. The key English-speaker pitfall is the particle — English 'in charge OF' tempts learners to use 에, but Korean treats the responsibility as a direct object, so it is 마케팅을 담당해요, never 마케팅에 담당해요.

Don't substitute 담당하다 for a casual 'I'll do it' among friends; it sounds like a formal job assignment. For volunteering warmly, 맡다 (제가 맡을게요) fits better.

usage: 역할(役割) 'role'; 맡다 collocates with roles, parts, and duties you personally accept.
책임 'responsibility' + 맡다 = assume responsibility; common when stepping up for a team.
Causative pair (맡 + 기): you hand the task to another person — 저한테 맡기세요 'leave it to me'.
Everyday non-work sense — 맡다 also means 'hold/reserve' a spot: 자리 좀 맡아 줘.
examples: 그 일은 제가 맡을게요.
I'll take that on.
-(으)ㄹ게요 = a willing commitment to the listener; sounds proactive and reliable.
이번 행사는 김 대리가 맡았어요.
Assistant Manager Kim took charge of this event.
Past 맡았어요 (stem ㅌ + 아) reports who got the assignment — note it is NOT 마랐어요.
부장님이 저한테 그 프로젝트를 맡기셨어요.
The department head entrusted me with that project.
맡기다 = causative 'hand over/entrust'; 저한테 marks the receiver — contrast with plain 맡다.
nuance: 맡다 is the everyday native-Korean verb for taking on a role or responsibility — a task, a project, a part, even a saved seat. It feels more personal and active than the Sino-Korean 담당하다: where 담당하다 is the official 'assigned to me' on an org chart, 맡다 is the warm, often-volunteered 'I'll take this', so 제가 맡을게요 sounds team-friendly and proactive in a meeting. Crucial spelling and conjugation point: the stem ends in ㅌ, and it is a plain regular verb, NOT a ㄷ-irregular — so it stays 맡아요 / 맡았어요 / 맡을게요, and learners who mistakenly 'soften' the ㅌ to ㄹ (마라요, 마랐어요) are simply wrong. Its causative partner 맡기다 ('to entrust/hand over') flips the direction: you 맡다 a job yourself, but you 맡기다 it to someone else (저한테 맡기세요). Habitual collocations: 역할을 맡다, 책임을 맡다, 업무를 맡다, 자리를 맡다.

usage: to report to the team leader
The recipient (a superior) takes the honorific dative 께; 께 is the polite form of 에게/한테.
to report (humbly, up to a senior)
보고 + 드리다 (humble 'give'); use when YOU report to someone above you: 부장님께 보고드릴게요.
The content reported takes 을/를: 결과를 / 진행 상황을 보고하다.
보고 + 서(書) 'document'; the written deliverable — 보고서를 작성하다 'write up a report'.
examples: 결과를 보고했어요.
I reported the results.
Base pattern: 〈content〉을/를 보고하다. Clean and factual.
문제가 생기면 바로 보고해 주세요.
If a problem comes up, please report it right away.
바로 = immediately; a very common instruction from a manager to staff.
이 내용은 부장님께 직접 보고드리겠습니다.
I'll report this directly to the manager myself.
보고드리겠습니다 = humble 보고드리다 + formal will; 께 marks the senior recipient.
nuance: 보고하다 is the formal verb for reporting information up a hierarchy — to a boss, a client, or headquarters. The hanja 報告 is 報 'to inform/requite' + 告 'to tell/announce', a doubled 'make known' that signals officialness. In Korea's hierarchy-conscious workplaces, 보고 (the report itself) is a weighty ritual, which is why you very often switch to the humble 보고드리다 when the listener outranks you. Grammar to nail: the recipient takes 께/에게(한테) and the content takes 을/를 (팀장님께 결과를 보고했어요). The decisive synonym contrast is with 말하다 / 알려주다: those are neutral 'tell / let know' for peers and friends, whereas 보고하다 frames the act as an upward, accountable report. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold — English 'report' covers casual gossip ('did you hear?'), but 보고하다 does NOT, so telling a friend news is 말하다/알려주다, not 보고하다; and learners forget to elevate to 보고드리다 when reporting to a senior.

usage: 대로 = 'in accordance with'; 계획대로 / 예정대로 진행하다 are set business phrases.
to be underway / proceed (on its own)
Passive pair: YOU 진행하다 it, but the process 진행돼요 by itself — 잘 진행되고 있어요.
진행 + 상황 'situation' = how far along something is: 진행 상황을 공유하다 'share the status'.
With events, 진행하다 also means 'to MC / run' it; 진행자 = the host/emcee.
examples: 일단 계획대로 진행할게요.
For now I'll proceed as planned.
일단 = 'for now / first off'; -(으)ㄹ게요 commits you to moving it forward.
지금 어디까지 진행됐어요?
How far along is it now?
Uses the passive 진행되다 — literally 'up to where has it progressed?', a standard status check.
다음 단계를 진행하기 전에 한번 확인해 주세요.
Please double-check before we proceed to the next step.
단계 = stage; -기 전에 = 'before doing'. Active 진행하다 = you carry it forward.
nuance: 진행하다 means to push a task, process, project, or event forward — 'carry out / proceed with' — and it saturates Korean office life. The hanja 進行 is 進 'advance' + 行 'go/move', literally 'advance-and-go', a forward motion that fits a multi-step process. The single most important thing to master is the active/passive pair: active 진행하다 means YOU drive it (제가 진행할게요 'I'll move it forward'), while passive 진행되다 means it is underway by itself (잘 진행되고 있어요 'it's going well') — mixing these up is the classic learner error. A useful contrast is with 마치다/끝내다 (to finish): 진행하다 is about the ongoing middle of a process with stages, not the endpoint, so don't use it for completing a single discrete action. With events it gains a second sense, 'to host/run', giving 진행자 (MC). Habitual collocations: 계획대로 진행하다, 예정대로 진행되다, 진행 상황, 절차를 진행하다.

Don't use 진행하다 for finishing one small action — it implies an ongoing, staged process. To complete a discrete task use 끝내다/마치다.

usage: Transitive: the thing you conclude takes 을/를 — 업무를 / 일을 / 수업을 마치다.
Set formal closing line for meetings and events; the announcer's standard wrap-up.
무사히 'safely/uneventfully' is the natural adverb with completing a big undertaking.
마친 뒤에 / 마치고 = 'having finished, then'; smoothly chains the next action.
examples: 오늘 일을 다 마쳤어요.
I finished all my work today.
다 = 'all'; past 마쳤어요 (ㅊ + ㅕ). Slightly formal, good for work or study.
발표를 마친 뒤에 질문을 받을게요.
I'll take questions after I finish the presentation.
-(으)ㄴ 뒤에 = 'after doing'; classic presentation phrasing.
이번 분기 보고서를 무사히 마쳤습니다.
I successfully finished this quarter's report.
무사히 + 마치다 = brought a big task to a clean close; formal -습니다 for a report-out.
nuance: 마치다 means to finish or conclude something properly — your workday, a meeting, a report, a course of study. It is transitive (it takes an object: 일을 마치다) and carries a slightly formal, ceremonial 'bring to a proper close' flavor, which is exactly why public announcements use 마치겠습니다. Two contrasts a learner must hold apart. First, against 끝내다: both are transitive 'finish it', but 마치다 is more bookish and dignified (a meeting, a ceremony, a semester), while 끝내다 is the casual, hands-on 'get it done' of daily office chatter. Second, and the real pitfall, against 끝나다: 끝나다 is INTRANSITIVE ('it ends by itself') and takes no object, so 'the work ended' is 일이 끝났어요, never 일을 마쳤어요 unless you are the one actively concluding it. Conjugation: the stem 마치- + 어 contracts to 마쳐요 / 마쳤어요. Habitual collocations: 일을 마치다, 회의를 마치다, 학업을 마치다, 무사히 마치다.

Don't reach for 마치다 in very casual coworker talk; it sounds formal/ceremonial. For 'let me just wrap this up', 끝내다 (이것만 끝내고 갈게요) is more natural.

usage: Transitive: 일을 / 숙제를 / 회의를 끝내다 — you actively bring it to an end.
Intransitive partner: 일이 끝났어요 'the work ended'; no object, just happens.
안에 'within (a time)' + 끝내다 expresses deadline pressure: 오늘 안에 끝내야 해요.
빨리/얼른 + 끝내다 is the everyday 'let's get it done fast' of coworker talk.
examples: 이것만 끝내고 갈게요.
Let me just finish this and then go.
만 = 'just this'; -고 갈게요 chains 'finish, then leave'. Very natural daily phrase.
일을 다 못 끝냈어요.
I couldn't finish all the work.
못 + 끝내다 = 'couldn't manage to finish'; 다 = all. Past is 끝냈어요 (stem 끝내-).
회의를 30분 안에 끝낼 수 있을까요?
Can we wrap up the meeting within 30 minutes?
-(으)ㄹ 수 있을까요 = 'do you think we can ~?'; practical scheduling question.
nuance: 끝내다 is the active, everyday verb for finishing or wrapping something up — you make it end. It is the transitive causative of 끝나다: the pair 끝내다 / 끝나다 is the cleanest minimal contrast in the whole 'finish' family, and getting it right is the core skill here. 끝내다 takes an object and means YOU end it (숙제를 끝냈어요 'I finished the homework'); 끝나다 is intransitive and means it ends by itself (수업이 끝났어요 'class ended'). Against 마치다, 끝내다 is the more casual, task-focused choice — perfect for daily office lines like 이것만 끝내고 갈게요 — whereas 마치다 is bookish and ceremonial. (Note 끝내다 also has a slang sense: 끝내주다 / 끝내준다 = 'awesome', literally 'it finishes you off'.) Conjugation is easy and regular: stem 끝내- gives past 끝냈어요. Habitual collocations: 일을 끝내다, 숙제를 끝내다, 빨리 끝내다, 오늘 안에 끝내다.

Conjugation is easy and regular: stem 끝내- gives past 끝냈어요.

mistakes: Don't swap transitive 끝내다 (you finish it) with intransitive 끝나다 (it finishes): 숙제를 끝냈어요 (object + 끝내다) vs. 수업이 끝났어요 (subject + 끝나다). Saying 수업을 끝났어요 is a classic particle/verb mismatch.
Past tense spelling: it's 끝냈어요 (stem 끝내- + 었), not 끝났어요 — 끝났어요 belongs to 끝나다. Mixing the two stems garbles which verb you mean.

usage: 검토하다 collocates with 서류 / 계약서 / 제안서 / 자료 — things you scrutinize before deciding.
검토 + 중 'in the middle of'; a polite, face-saving 'we're still deciding': 내부적으로 검토 중입니다.
-아/어 보다 softens it to 'let me look into it' before committing to an answer.
Diplomatic set phrase — a soft yes-ish 'we'll look at it positively', common in negotiations.
examples: 이 제안서 좀 검토해 주시겠어요?
Could you review this proposal?
-아/어 주시겠어요 = polite request; 좀 softens it. Standard for asking a colleague to check something.
내부적으로 검토 중입니다.
We're reviewing it internally.
검토 중 = 'under review'; a polished way to say 'no decision yet' without refusing.
꼼꼼하게 검토했는데 문제는 없었어요.
I reviewed it carefully and there were no problems.
꼼꼼하게 = thoroughly/meticulously, a prized work trait; -는데 sets up the result.
nuance: 검토하다 means to review or examine something carefully — documents, proposals, plans, contracts — usually before approving or deciding. The hanja 檢討 is 檢 'inspect/examine' + 討 'investigate/discuss', a deliberate double 'scrutinize', which is why it sounds polished and weighty. The phrase 검토 중이에요 ('it's under review') is a genuinely useful, face-saving way to say a decision hasn't been made yet, and 긍정적으로 검토하겠습니다 is diplomatic for a soft maybe-yes. The crucial synonym contrast is with 확인하다: 확인하다 is a quick 'check/confirm' a fact, a time, or a number, while 검토하다 implies sustained, careful inspection with judgment to follow — so confirming a meeting time is 확인하다, never 검토하다. Compare also 검사하다 (to inspect/test, often physical or for defects) and 살펴보다 (to look over, less official). Habitual collocations: 계약서를 검토하다, 검토 중, 검토 의견, 꼼꼼하게 검토하다.

usage: 야근 + 수당 'allowance'; the money you get for staying late — a frequent gripe topic.
Noun 야근 + 잦다 'be frequent' is how people complain: 요즘 야근이 너무 잦아요.
When 야근 stretches till dawn, it becomes 밤샘(근무); 밤새다 = 'stay up all night'.
야근 = staying past hours on a day job; 야간근무 = a scheduled night shift (e.g. nurses, factories).
examples: 오늘도 야근해요.
I'm working late again today.
오늘도 'again today' nails the weary office mood; present tense for a recurring reality.
마감 때문에 이번 주 내내 야근했어요.
I worked late all week because of the deadline.
때문에 = 'because of'; 내내 = 'the whole time/all through'. 마감 = deadline.
야근하지 말고 얼른 들어가세요.
Don't work late, head home soon.
-지 말고 = 'don't ~ but rather'; 들어가다 here = 'go home'. A caring thing to say to a coworker.
nuance: 야근하다 is the verb every Korean office worker knows: to stay and work into the evening, past regular hours. The hanja 夜勤 is 夜 'night' + 勤 'work/service' (the same 勤 as in 근무), literally 'night-work'. Its form is neutral, but in real use it almost always carries a tired, faintly complaining tone, because overtime is a charged feature of Korean work culture; the noun 야근 anchors a whole vocabulary of grievance — 야근 수당 (OT pay), 야근 잦아요 (lots of overtime), 칼퇴 (leaving right on time, the dream). The sharp boundary is against 야간근무: 야근 is staying late on an otherwise daytime job, whereas 야간근무 is a scheduled night shift (nurses, security, factory lines). Don't equate it with English 'overtime' as a contractual category either — that abstract concept is 초과근무 / 시간 외 근무. And for an all-nighter it escalates to 밤샘. Habitual collocations: 야근하다, 야근 수당, 야근이 잦다, 야근 안 하다.

usage: Often just 퇴사하다 alone; if stated, the company can take 를 or appear with 에서.
Direct opposites: 입사(入社) 'enter a company' / 퇴사(退社) 'exit a company'. Learn as a pair.
What you must do before 퇴사: 인수인계 'receive-and-pass-on' your work to a successor.
이직(移職) = move to another job; 퇴사 is leaving, 이직 is leaving for a new employer.
examples: 저 다음 달에 퇴사해요.
I'm leaving the company next month.
Present tense for a fixed plan; 저 fronts 'as for me'. The standard way to announce it.
퇴사하기 전에 인수인계를 해야 해요.
Before resigning I have to hand over my work.
-기 전에 = 'before doing'; 인수인계 is the obligatory pre-departure step.
김 대리님 퇴사하셨대요.
I heard Assistant Manager Kim resigned.
-셨대요 = honorific 시 + reported -대요 'I heard that ~'; classic office grapevine.
nuance: 퇴사하다 means to leave your company — to resign or quit for good. The hanja 退社 is 退 'retreat/withdraw' + 社 'company', literally 'withdraw from the company', and it is the exact mirror of 입사하다 (入社, 'enter the company'), so the two are best memorized as a set. 퇴사 is a culturally loaded, much-discussed topic among younger Korean workers, traveling with 이직 (移職, changing jobs), 인수인계 (handover), and 퇴사 통보 (notice of resignation). The contrast with near-synonym 그만두다 ('quit/stop') is one of register: 그만두다 is plainer and broader (you can 그만두다 anything — a job, a hobby, smoking), while 퇴사하다 is the clean, specific corporate term for leaving employment. The big English-speaker pitfall is confusing 퇴사하다 with 퇴근하다: they look and sound alike but 퇴사하다 ENDS your employment, while 퇴근하다 just means going home at the end of a workday (its opposite is 출근하다). Habitual collocations: 퇴사하다, 퇴사 통보, 퇴사 사유, 퇴사 후.

퇴사하다 vs 입사하다 direction: 퇴사(退) is leaving, 입사(入) is joining. Don't reverse them — 작년에 퇴사했어요 means you LEFT last year, not started.

usage: The company takes 에 (the destination you enter), NOT 을/를: 이 회사에 입사했어요.
people who joined the same year
입사 + 동기 'same period'; your cohort — a meaningful bond in Korean work life.
to join as a new hire
신입 'new recruit' + 으로 'as'; contrast 경력으로 입사하다 = join as an experienced hire.
입사 + 지원 'apply/support' = applying to a company; 입사 지원서 = the application form.
examples: 작년에 이 회사에 입사했어요.
I joined this company last year.
Note 에 on 회사 (destination), not 를. The base 'I joined ~' frame.
언제 입사하셨어요?
When did you join the company?
Honorific 하셨어요 to a coworker; a friendly, common get-to-know-you question.
원하던 회사에 입사하게 돼서 정말 기뻐요.
I'm so happy I got into the company I wanted.
원하던 = 'that I'd wanted'; -게 돼서 = 'because it came to be that' — humble, gladdened tone.
nuance: 입사하다 means to join a company as an employee — your starting point in a job, the exact mirror image of 퇴사하다 (to leave). The hanja 入社 is 入 'enter' + 社 'company', literally 'enter the company', and because 入 is a verb of entering, the company you join takes the destination particle 에 (이 회사에 입사하다) — this is the number-one English-speaker pitfall, since English 'join the company' tempts you toward the object 를 (회사를 입사하다 is wrong). It anchors a cluster of new-employee vocabulary you'll hear daily: 신입 (new hire), 입사 동기 (people who joined the same year, a real social bond), 입사 지원 (job application), 입사 시험/면접 (entrance exam/interview). A subtle synonym note: 입사하다 specifically means entering a COMPANY, whereas 취직하다/취업하다 means 'to get employed / land a job' more generally, and 입학하다 (入學) is the parallel word for entering a SCHOOL — don't cross the 社/學 wires. Best learned paired with 퇴사하다 so you can narrate both ends of a job.

usage: to have a meeting with the team
The people you meet with take (이)랑 / 와 / 과: 팀이랑 / 팀과 회의해요.
Noun 회의 + 중 'in the middle of'; the text you send all day: 지금 회의 중이에요.
잡다 'to grab/fix' + 회의 = schedule one: 내일로 회의 잡을게요 'I'll set the meeting for tomorrow'.
회의 + 실(室) 'room'; book it as 회의실 예약 — basic office-logistics vocab.
examples: 오후에 팀이랑 회의해요.
I have a meeting with my team this afternoon.
(이)랑 marks who you meet with; casual-polite 회의해요. Simple schedule statement.
지금 회의 중이라 나중에 전화할게요.
I'm in a meeting now, so I'll call later.
회의 중이라 = 'because I'm in a meeting'; uses the noun 회의, not the verb. Texted constantly.
다 같이 모여서 한번 회의해 봅시다.
Let's all get together and have a meeting.
-아/어 봅시다 = 'let's try ~'; -ㅂ시다 is a confident formal suggestion to the team.
nuance: 회의하다 means to hold or have a meeting — the daily texture of office life. The hanja 會議 is 會 'gather/assemble' + 議 'discuss/deliberate', literally 'gather-and-deliberate', which captures that it implies a real, purposeful, usually scheduled discussion rather than idle talk. In practice the bare noun 회의 surfaces even more than the verb: 회의 중이에요 (in a meeting), 회의 잡다 (set a meeting), 회의실 (meeting room), 회의록 (meeting minutes). Grammar to nail: co-participants take (이)랑/와/과 (팀이랑 회의해요), and the topic discussed often rides along with -에 대해(서) (그 문제에 대해 회의했어요). The decisive synonym contrast is with 얘기하다/이야기하다: those mean simply 'talk/chat', right for a two-minute hallway exchange, whereas 회의하다 frames it as a formal sit-down — so don't say 회의하다 for a quick chat (use 잠깐 얘기하다). Compare also 상의하다/논의하다 (to consult/deliberate on a matter), which stress the discussing more than the gathering.
